# Dīghanakha Sutta (MN 74 (PTS MN i 497))
**ID:** MN 74 (PTS MN i 497)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Dīghanakha Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** With Dīghanakha

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Dīghanakha Sutta* is the 74th discourse of the *Majjhima Nikāya* (PTS MN i 497) [SuttaCentral]. In this discourse, the wanderer (or renouncer) Dīghanakha approaches the Buddha and asserts the skeptical view that "nothing is acceptable to me" (*sabbam me na khamati*) [Anderson 1999]. In response, the Buddha critiques this position alongside its alternatives ("everything is acceptable to me" and "some things are acceptable and some are not"), demonstrating how extreme skepticism and the grasping of views lead to disputation [Anderson 1999; Emmanuel 2013]. Rather than becoming trapped in conceptual abstractions, the Buddha redirects attention to living experience by examining the physical body and the three types of feeling (pleasant, painful, and neutral), which arise in dependence on contact and are mutually exclusive [SuttaCentral; Anālayo 2014; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. The discourse famously concludes with Sāriputta—standing nearby and reflecting on the Buddha's instruction to abandon and let go through direct insight—attaining full liberation (arahantship), while Dīghanakha attains the "dhamma-eye" (stream-entry) [Anālayo 2010; Anderson 1999; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. The text also emphasizes that a liberated adept uses conventional speech without grasping or adhering to it [Powers 2016; Emmanuel 2013].
Curated parallels recorded on SuttaCentral include two versions in the Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* (SĀ 969 and SĀ² 203), the *Avadānaśataka* (no. 99), fragments in the Tibetan Vinaya (*mu-kd-eimer* / *Pravrajyāvastu*), several Chinese treatises including the *Mahāprajñāpāramitopadeśa* (T 1509) and the *Mahāvibhāṣā* (T 1545), as well as Sanskrit fragments (SF 81 and SF 133) [SuttaCentral; Anālayo 2014]. In addition, early Sanskrit Buddhist literature such as the *Mahāvastu* preserves ancient recensions of the discourse [Lamotte 1988; Nariman 1919]. DharmaNexus text-reuse computations agree with alignments to the Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* (T 99, T 100), the Tibetan *Vinayavastu* (D 0001), the Sanskrit *Śayanāsanavastu*, and the *Divyāvadāna* [DharmaNexus]. Internally within the Pali canon, DharmaNexus aligns the sutta extensively with the *Khandha Saṃyutta* (SN 22), the *Saḷāyatana Saṃyutta* (SN 35), the *Apaṇṇaka Sutta* (MN 60), the *Mahākhandhaka* (Kd 1), and discourses in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* [DharmaNexus].
